[C21] Intake pipeline. Our intake pipeline turns scanned invoices into machine-readable fields. Page images pass through character recognition, then a layout model locates tables and headings, and the result is written out as structured JSON for downstream search. Each stage records a confidence value, and pages falling below a set confidence are routed to a human reviewer instead of being indexed automatically. The pipeline handles about nine thousand pages an hour on a single server, and it keeps the original image alongside the extracted text so that reviewers can compare the two side by side when a field looks suspicious.

[C22] Table recovery. Rebuilding rows and columns from ruled and unruled grids is the hardest step. The recovery model looks for alignment cues and repeated whitespace, then assigns each cell to a header. Merged cells still cause roughly one error in forty tables, and tables that span two pages are often read as two separate tables with duplicated headers. The team improved results by teaching the model to recognise running headers and repeated column titles, and by adding a repair step that joins tables when the last row of one page continues on the next. Nested tables and tables rotated sideways remain unsolved problems.

[C23] Parsing tools bake-off. In the third-quarter bake-off we compared three parsing tools: Loomdoc, Pagekiln, and Stitchreader. Each was run on the same 1,200 pages, drawn from invoices, receipts, contracts and handwritten forms. Stitchreader was fastest, while Pagekiln produced the cleanest tables. Loomdoc sat in the middle on both measures but handled unusual fonts better than either rival. The panel scored each tool on speed, accuracy, memory use and ease of setup, and agreed that no single product won every category. A follow-up study will repeat the comparison on a larger and more varied set of documents.

[C24] Chunking strategy. Extracted text is split into overlapping windows of 512 tokens with a 64-token overlap. Headings are kept with the paragraph that follows them so that a retrieved passage still carries its context. Very short fragments are merged into their neighbours, and tables are kept whole where possible so that a row is never separated from its header. The team tested windows from 128 to 2,048 tokens and found that retrieval quality rose until about 512 tokens and then flattened, while larger windows made answers vaguer and more expensive to generate. The settings are stored with each chunk so that they can be audited later.

[C25] Evaluation results. On the Halden receipts set, Pagekiln scored 0.91 field-level F1 and Loomdoc scored 0.87. Stitchreader scored 0.82 but finished in a third of the time. Handwritten pages lowered every score by about nine points, and faded thermal receipts caused the most failures. The team concluded that table-heavy documents should go to Pagekiln, while high-volume simple pages could safely use Stitchreader. Scores were computed by matching extracted fields to a hand-checked answer key, and a field counted as correct only if the text and its position both matched. Confidence intervals were within two points for every tool.
